newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Golkar poised for biggest poll win.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Golkar poised for biggest poll win.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar headed on Friday for its biggest election win in nearly three decades in power after a poll in which it was assured of victory even before a vote was cast.
But political analysts foresaw no government or policy changes after an election campaign marred by the worst political violence in President Suharto's 30-year rule.
"The results are not surprising," one diplomatic analyst said following Thursday's poll for 425 elected parliamentary seats.
The stock market jumped in early trading but then lost ground on news of an election-related riot on the island of Madura off east Java after the polls closed on Thursday.
The composite index remained up on the day, while the rupiah strengthened against the dollar.
By early afternoon, Golkar had won 73.61 percent of just over 100 million votes counted out of a potential 125 million.

Of the two other groups allowed to contest the polls, held every five years, Golkar's main campaign opponent, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) had 23.47 percent, while the badly-split Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) fell to a disastrous 2.92 percent from 15 percent in 1992.

The PDI was swamped following a leadership struggle after party chief Megawati Sukarnoputri, eldest daughter of Indonesia's founding president Sukarno, was ousted by a government-backed faction last year.
Political analysts said her opponent, deputy speaker of parliament Surjadi, had lacked credibility and the party had lost heavily as a result. Megawati was not immediately available for comment.
Surjadi said that if the vote count was accurate, "the drastic drop in PDI votes is a major cause for concern". He said the party would discuss it at a meeting next Tuesday.
Indonesia's Independent Election Monitoring Comittee (KIPP) said on Friday it had found evidence of systematic violations of the general election rules during its monitoring of Thursday's poll.

KIPP, a group of leading dissidents and government critics, said its 8,000 volunteers in 47 cities in 17 provinces had found instances of multiple voting, intimidation of party witnesses, discrimination in the treatment of voters and various procedural irregulaties.
Most of the violence in the 27-day campaign, primarily centred on Java island where 60 percent of the country's 200 million people live, was between Golkar and PPP partisans.
Political and financial analysts had feared more violence, particularly in Jakarta, if PPP supporters felt they had been cheated in the polls.

PPP campaign manager Jusuf Sjakir told a news conference there had been a number of voting irregularities and the party -- which took 17 percent of the vote in 1992 -- would decide at a meeting next Thursday whether it accepted the poll result.
The Maduran rioters burned houses, offices and a church in anger over Golkar's vote share in the strongly Moslem area, but police and residents said the situation was calm on Friday.

East Timor was worst hit by election violence. Police said 17 people died on Wednesday and Thursday following attacks by guerrillas opposed to Jakarta's rule of the former Portuguese colony, annexed by Indonesia in 1976.
Overall, the country was calm on Friday with only isolated incidents reported in the archipelago of 17,500 islands spread over 5,000 km (3,000 miles) along the equator.
Some analysts said Golkar and the PPP had both benefitted from the collapse of the PDI.

Before the 27-day election campaign, the only time active politics are permitted by the government, Golkar set a target of just over 70 percent of the vote. It received 68 percent in the last elections in 1992, down from a peak of 73.17 in 1987.

Political analysts were also watching for the number of spoiled ballots and abstentions by dissidents -- known collectively in Indonesia as Golput, or the White Party. There was no immediate indication of the size Golput, which amounted to around three-to-four percent in 1992.
Analysts said President Suharto could be well satisfied with Golkar's vote, which would ease his way to an expected seventh five-year term in March next year.
A senior Asian diplomat, however, said Thursday's elections should not be seen as a vote on Suharto himself.
"The election is not a mandate for Suharto, it's not a judgement on him, but it does make it easier for Suharto to be re-elected," he said.
Analysts generally see the presidential poll next year as the key election for the country, with keen interest in who the 75-year-old president will select as a running mate and potential successor.
